title: Unit 8: Applications of Integration

topics.name: Average value, motion, and accumulation
covers: Determining the average value of a function using definite integrals

topics.name: Volume and arc length
covers: Determining volume with cross-sections, the disc method, and the washer method
Determining the length of a planar curve using a definite integral

guide.title: Applications of integration: review guide
guide.intro: Integrals add up small pieces. This unit uses that idea for average values, motion along a line, accumulation, the area between curves, volumes of solids, and (in BC) the length of a curve.

sections.title: Average value, motion, and accumulation
body: The average value of f on [a, b] is (1/(b − a)) ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx.
For motion along a line, ∫ v(t) dt is the displacement and ∫ |v(t)| dt is the total distance. Position at time b = position at time a + ∫ from a to b of v(t) dt.
points: For total distance, split the integral where v changes sign, or integrate |v|.
Average value is not the average of the endpoint values.
Always add the initial amount when finding an amount, not just a change.

sections.title: Area between curves
body: Area = ∫ (top − bottom) dx between the curves' intersection points. If the curves cross inside the interval, split the integral so the difference stays positive.
When the region is easier to describe left-to-right, integrate in y: area = ∫ (right − left) dy.
points: Find the intersection points first; they are usually the limits.
A negative result means top and bottom were reversed.
Curves given as x = g(y) usually call for integrating with respect to y.

sections.title: Volume and arc length
body: Cross sections: V = ∫ A(x) dx, where A(x) is the area of a slice (for a square with side s, A = s²). Disc method: V = π ∫ R(x)² dx. Washer method: V = π ∫ (R(x)² − r(x)²) dx, with outer radius R and inner radius r.
Arc length (BC): the length of y = f(x) from a to b is ∫ from a to b of √(1 + f′(x)²) dx.
points: Square each radius separately in the washer method: R² − r², not (R − r)².
Cross sections of a base region don't include π unless the slices are circles.
Measure radii from the axis of rotation.

example.prompt: The region between y = √x and the x-axis on [0, 4] is revolved about the x-axis. Find the volume.
example.solution: Disc method with R = √x: V = π ∫ from 0 to 4 of x dx = π · 16/2 = 8π.

misconceptions: “∫ v dt gives the total distance.”
It gives displacement; total distance needs ∫ |v| dt.
It subtracts the squared radii: R² − r².
Use the integral divided by the interval's length.
That's a signed area; arc length is ∫ √(1 + f′(x)²) dx.

questions.prompt: What is the average value of f(x) = x² on [0, 3]?
choiceExplanations: 9 is the integral; it still needs dividing by the interval length 3.
2.25 is f(1.5), the value at the midpoint.
4.5 averages the endpoint values f(0) = 0 and f(3) = 9.

questions.prompt: A particle's velocity is v(t) = t² − 4 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 3. What total distance does it travel?
questions.explanation: v changes sign at t = 2. Distance = ∫ from 0 to 2 of (4 − t²) dt + ∫ from 2 to 3 of (t² − 4) dt = 16/3 + 7/3 = 23/3.
choiceExplanations: 5 is v(3), the velocity at the end.
3 is the size of the displacement; it misses the backtracking.
−3 is the displacement, ∫ from 0 to 3 of v dt.

questions.prompt: A particle has velocity v(t) = 3t² − 2t and position x(0) = 5. What is x(2)?
choiceExplanations: 8 is v(2), the velocity at t = 2.
4 is the displacement only; it forgets the starting position 5.
13 adds v(2) to the starting position instead of integrating.

questions.prompt: What is the area of the region between y = x and y = x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1?
questions.explanation: On [0, 1], x ≥ x², so the area is ∫ from 0 to 1 of (x − x²) dx = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6.
choiceExplanations: 1/3 is the area under y = x² alone.
1/2 is the area under y = x alone.
An area can't be negative; this subtracts the curves in the wrong order.

questions.prompt: What is the area of the region bounded by x = y² and x = y + 2?
questions.explanation: The curves meet where y² = y + 2, at y = −1 and y = 2. The line is on the right, so the area is ∫ from −1 to 2 of (y + 2 − y²) dy = 9/2.
choiceExplanations: This subtracts in the wrong order; an area is positive.
10/3 integrates only from y = 0 to y = 2.
7/6 integrates only from y = −1 to y = 0.

questions.prompt: The region under y = √x on [0, 4] is revolved about the x-axis. What is the volume of the solid?
questions.explanation: Disc method: V = π ∫ from 0 to 4 of (√x)² dx = π ∫ from 0 to 4 of x dx = 8π.
choiceExplanations: 8 leaves out the π from each disc's area.
16π forgets the 1/2 in ∫ x dx = x²/2.
16π/3 integrates the radius √x instead of its square.

questions.prompt: The region between y = x and y = x² on [0, 1] is revolved about the x-axis. What is the volume of the solid?
questions.explanation: Washer method with R = x and r = x²: V = π ∫ from 0 to 1 of (x² − x⁴) dx = π(1/3 − 1/5) = 2π/15.
choiceExplanations: 2/15 leaves out π.
π/6 multiplies the region's area by π, which isn't a volume formula.
π/30 squares the difference, (x − x²)², instead of subtracting the squares.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and official topics come from the linked College Board page, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-11-08); that page was used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: A solid's base is the region between y = 1 − x² and the x-axis. Cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are squares. What is its volume?
questions.explanation: Each square has side 1 − x², so V = ∫ from −1 to 1 of (1 − x²)² dx = 2∫ from 0 to 1 of (1 − 2x² + x⁴) dx = 2(8/15) = 16/15.
choiceExplanations: 8/15 integrates only from 0 to 1, half the base.
4/3 is the area of the base, not the volume.
16π/15 is the volume when the region is revolved about the x-axis (disc method); square slices have no π.

questions.prompt: What is the length of the curve y = (2/3)x^(3/2) from x = 0 to x = 3?
choiceExplanations: 16/3 forgets to subtract the antiderivative's value at x = 0.
2√3 is y(3), the curve's rise, not its length.
15/2 integrates 1 + (y′)² without the square root.
